---
title: "Why simulate a breeding program?"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 110)
```

Breeders make design decisions all the time. How many lines should go to the
advanced trial? How many parents should be recycled? Is a second location
worth more than a second rep? Quantitative genetics gives formulas for some of
these questions, and field data answer others after many years. Simulation
fills the gap. You build a model of your program on the computer, run it many
times, and look at what tends to happen.

This article is for readers who have never run a breeding simulation. It
uses [AlphaSimR](https://cran.r-project.org/package=AlphaSimR) to simulate the
genetics and tidyagsim to organize the experiment. By the end you will have
checked a simulation against the breeder's equation and watched it answer a
question the equation cannot.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyagsim)
library(AlphaSimR)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## One cycle of selection

Start with the simplest breeding program there is. Grow 200 inbred lines and
measure them, keep the best `n_select`, intermate those lines, and look at
the offspring. In AlphaSimR that is three function calls. tidyagsim wraps
them in `alphasim_program()`, which turns the script into a *simulation spec*,
a recipe tidyagsim can run as many times as you like:

```{r}
recurrent <- alphasim_program(
  function(founders, SP, n_select, cycles) {
    tracker <- asr_tracker(founders)               # remembers where we started
    pop <- founders
    for (cycle in seq_len(cycles)) {
      pop <- setPheno(pop)                         # grow and measure every plant
      parents <- selectInd(pop, n_select)          # keep the best n_select
      pop <- randCross(parents, nCrosses = 200)    # intermate them: 200 offspring
      tracker$record(pop, year = cycle, cost = 200 * 15)
    }
    asr_summary(tracker)                           # gain, variance, cost, ...
  },
  n_select = 20, cycles = 1,
  founders = asr_founders(n_founders = 200, n_chr = 10, seg_sites = 100, plot_h2 = 0.3)
)
recurrent
```

The function describes **one replicate**, a single run of the program from new
founders. `asr_founders()` describes those founders: 200 inbred lines, a trait
controlled by many QTL, and a single-plot heritability of 0.3. Genetic values
are reported in units of the founders' genetic standard deviation (SD). A gain
of 1 means the offspring are one founder genetic SD better than the founders.

## Run it once, then run it 200 times

`fit_resamples()` runs a spec on a set of replicates. Each replicate gets its
own random seed, and so its own founders and its own luck:

```{r}
one <- fit_resamples(recurrent, sim_replicates(1))
collect_metrics(one)
```

That number is one draw. Run it again with a different seed and you will get
a different answer. To see how much it varies, run 200 replicates:

```{r}
many <- fit_resamples(recurrent, sim_replicates(200, seed = 1))
gains <- collect_metrics(many, summarize = FALSE)
```

The breeder's equation predicts the response to one cycle of truncation
selection: R = *i h*² σ~P~, or *i h* in genetic SDs. Here *i* is the
selection intensity for keeping 20 of 200 and *h*² is 0.3:

```{r}
p <- 20 / 200
i <- dnorm(qnorm(1 - p)) / p
predicted <- i * sqrt(0.3)
predicted
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Histogram of the gain from one cycle of selection in 200 replicates, centred on the breeder's equation prediction."}
ggplot(gains, aes(release_gain)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#4C78A8", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = predicted, linetype = 2, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(gains$release_gain), colour = "#E45756", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Gain from one cycle (founder genetic SDs)", y = "Replicates",
       title = "200 runs of the same program",
       subtitle = "Dashed: breeder's equation. Red: average of the simulations.")
```

Two lessons are in this picture:

1. **The simulation agrees with theory.** On average it lands where the
   breeder's equation says it should. A simulation is a model you can check.
2. **Any single run can mislead.** Individual runs range from
   `r round(min(gains$release_gain), 2)` to `r round(max(gains$release_gain), 2)`,
   so one run could suggest this design is half as good, or half again better,
   than it really is. One simulation is like one field trial at one location:
   an anecdote, not an answer. tidyagsim always runs many replicates and reports
   the average with its *Monte Carlo standard error*, the uncertainty that
   comes from running only a finite number of replicates.

```{r}
collect_metrics(many)
```

## A question the formula can't answer

The breeder's equation describes one generation. Over many cycles, selection
uses up genetic variance and small parent pools drift, so the best one-cycle
choice is not always the best long-term choice. Let's mark `n_select` with
`tune()`, which says "try several values of this", and follow the program for
15 cycles:

```{r}
long <- set_args(recurrent, n_select = tune(), cycles = 15)
long_res <- tune_grid(
  long,
  resamples = sim_replicates(30, seed = 1),
  grid = data.frame(n_select = c(4, 10, 25, 60)),
  control = control_sim(save_outcomes = TRUE)
)
```

`tune_grid()` ran every value of `n_select` on the same 30 seeds, so every
design started from the same 30 sets of founders. `collect_trajectories()`
gathers the yearly records:

```{r, fig.alt = "Average genetic gain over 15 cycles for four numbers of selected parents. Keeping 4 parents is level with the leaders for two cycles and then falls behind; 10 and 25 parents finish highest."}
traj <- collect_trajectories(long_res)
avg <- aggregate(cbind(mean, genetic_variance) ~ n_select + year, data = traj, FUN = mean)

ggplot(avg, aes(year, mean, colour = factor(n_select))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Cycle", y = "Mean genetic value (founder SDs)", colour = "Parents kept",
       title = "Strong selection wins early, then runs out of variance")
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Genetic variance remaining over 15 cycles; it falls fastest with 4 parents."}
ggplot(avg, aes(year, genetic_variance, colour = factor(n_select))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Cycle", y = "Genetic variance (fraction of founders')", colour = "Parents kept")
```

Keeping only 4 parents is level with the leaders for the first two cycles,
then falls behind as the genetic variance it needs runs out. Keeping 10 leads
for most of the run, and keeping 25 catches it by cycle 12 because it still has
variance to work with. Keeping 60 selects too weakly to keep up. Which design
is "best" depends on how long your horizon is. The breeder's equation cannot show this trade-off, and a field
experiment would take decades. The simulation took seconds.

## What you used

| Term | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| **spec** | the recipe: an AlphaSimR script plus its settings (`alphasim_program()`) |
| **replicate** | one run of the spec from new founders, set by a seed (`sim_replicates()`) |
| **design** | one combination of the settings you are choosing between (`n_select = 10`) |
| **`tune()`** | "try several values of this setting" |
| **metric** | a number each replicate reports, such as `release_gain` |
| **Monte Carlo SE** | how much the average would move if you reran with new seeds |

Next, [How many replicates do I need?](replicates.html) shows how to choose
the number of replicates, and why running every design on the same seeds
matters so much.
